claims.text: Rapid solidification or high-energy ball milling causes severe grain refinement and solute trapping in refractory multi-principal element alloys.
Annealing at 800–1000 °C can produce BCC+B2 decomposition in the proposed refractory alloy without substantial grain coarsening or Laves-phase nucleation.
The proposed processing route will produce grain sizes below 50 nm.
A BCC+B2 dual-phase structure can be stabilized by low-temperature annealing.
Maintaining VEC between 4.4 and 4.8 stabilizes B2 while suppressing Laves and other brittle intermetallic phases.
A VEC of 4.4–4.8 ensures ductility in the proposed refractory alloy.
Oxygen introduced during processing can cause oxide precipitation in a Nb-Mo-Ta-W-V-Ti refractory alloy.
TiO2 is the oxide observed in the cited NbMoTaWVTi processing study.
Ordered B2 precipitates with a characteristic size of 10–50 nm will form inside a disordered BCC matrix.
Sluggish diffusion inherent to multi-principal element alloys stabilizes the proposed nanoscale BCC+B2 structure.
Composition and annealing temperature control the length scale and stability of BCC+B2 decomposition.
The ordered B2 phase provides precipitation strengthening.
The disordered BCC matrix provides ductility in the proposed BCC+B2 refractory alloy.
A fine-grained BCC matrix can increase strength through grain-boundary strengthening.
Cr addition to HfMoTaTiZr causes formation of a Laves phase.
VEC-based composition tuning can prevent the Laves-phase formation observed after Cr addition.
The proposed nanocrystalline BCC+B2 alloy will have yield strength above 1750 MPa.
The proposed nanocrystalline BCC+B2 alloy will have fracture strain above 10%.
Conventional cast NbMoTaW is brittle at room temperature because of coarse grains and the absence of ductile phases.
Increasing SPS temperature to 1400 °C causes BCC grain coarsening in CrMoNbWV.

contradictions.description: High-energy ball milling is presented as an example of rapid solidification, although it is a solid-state mechanical-alloying process rather than a solidification process.

The claimed ductile VEC window of 4.4–4.8 conflicts with the cited criterion that ductile alloys have VEC ≤4.4 and brittle alloys have VEC ≥4.6; much of the proposed window therefore falls in the cited brittle regime.
